summary: EarthWatch is a web-based geographical data analysis tool that transforms complex datasets involving multiple variables into clear statistical graphs, maps and visual patterns. It identifies increasing and decreasing trends, showing how different factors influence geographical changes over time and across regions. Users can also upload their own datasets to generate visualisations and discover meaningful patterns. EarthWatch is particularly useful for researchers, geographers, environmental planners and other professionals who rely on analysing geographical patterns and trends to support informed decisions.
details:
EarthWatch: What Is Really Changing, Where, and How Sure Are We?

1. The problem

Flooding is a problem that cost millions of financial losses for Sarawak government and local residents. This problem inspired us to build a tool to help user to analyse similar or other disaster pattern, factors and moreover. However, a person who wants to know whether their own place is changing faces three obstacles:

  • Too many variables. Rain alone can be measured as a yearly total, a wettest day, or a count of heavy days, and each can tell a different story.
  • Different answers in different places. A variable can trend upward in one area and downward in another nearby, so a single regional number hides the pattern.
  • "Changing" is not the same as "significant". A line that slopes upward over 25 years may still be within normal year-to-year variation, and only a statistical test can say.

Our mission: help anyone, from a student to a council officer, pick a variable, see how it has changed in their own place, and learn how big the change is and how sure we can be.

2. The variables

EarthWatch works with variables in two groups. Each one is a layer the user can switch on.

Rain (source: NASA GPM IMERG, a mission; 0.1 degree, half-hourly)

  1. Heavy-rain days per year (days)
  2. Annual rainfall (mm)
  3. Wettest day of the year (mm)
  4. Days with 50 mm or more (days)

Land (source: NASA GLDAS 2.1, a model; 0.25 degree, 3-hourly)

  1. Air temperature (degrees C)
  2. Soil moisture, upper layer (kg per m2)
  3. Soil moisture, deeper layer (kg per m2)

3. What we built: EarthWatch

EarthWatch is one self-contained web page, with no server and no sign-in, that can be opened from a link on a phone. It has three parts.

3.1 Statistical visuals: trends and patterns

  • Layers you switch on and off, one for each variable.
  • Value or trend: each layer shows either the value for a chosen year, or the trend per decade.
  • Two-colour trend maps: rising areas in one colour and falling areas in another, with dots where the change is statistically significant, so a user sees at once where a variable goes opposite ways.
  • A year slider with play, so the change can be watched as it happens.
  • Click any spot or town to see its time series, a trend line, the size of the trend, and the test result in plain words.
  • Statistical charts for the clicked place: line graph, histogram, pie chart and bar chart (described in section 4).
  • An honest "About this data" panel: what each variable means, where it comes from, and what it cannot tell you.

Example of the message a user reads: "Around Sibu, annual rainfall has [increased / decreased / not changed significantly] by about [N] mm per decade." The numbers are filled in only after the analysis is run on the real data.

3.2 "What is changing here?"

When a user clicks a place, EarthWatch lists all variables for that place, ranked so that those with a significant trend come first, each with its direction and size. A user who does not know which variable to pick starts here and opens the ones that matter.

4. Data and method

  • Indices: heavy-rain days are counted against a fixed threshold, the 95th percentile of each place's own rainy days, so the trend measures change and not a moving target. Days and years use Malaysia local time.
  • How much: Sen's slope gives the rate of change per decade.
  • Significant or not: the Mann-Kendall test, corrected for year-to-year dependence, decides whether the trend is significant at 95%.
  • How sure: each trend is given with a 95% confidence interval, for example "about 12 mm per decade, likely between 3 and 21".
  • No forecasting and no risk score. Only measured and modelled history.
  • Labelled openly: which data are NASA's and which are not, and that GLDAS is a model.

Statistical charts

Each chart answers one question about the chosen variable and place.

  • Line graph: yearly values from 2000 to 2025, with the Sen's slope trend line and its 95% band. It answers: is it rising or falling, and how fast?
  • Histogram: how often each value occurs, with the first half of the record (2000 to 2012) drawn against the second half (2013 to 2025). It answers: has the whole spread of values shifted, or only the average?
  • Pie chart: the share of the study area where the trend is significantly rising, significantly falling, or not significant. It answers: how much of the region is changing?
  • Bar chart: the trend per decade for Sibu, Kapit, Bintulu and Kuching side by side, with error bars. It answers: which town is changing most, and do the towns agree?
  • Summary numbers: beside the charts, each variable and place has its mean, median, minimum, maximum and standard deviation.
  • Same data, same rules: every chart is drawn from the same yearly series used for the trend test, so a chart and a test result never disagree.

5. What users will learn, whatever the result

  • A variable has a significant trend: it is changing here, in this direction, by this much per decade.
  • No significant trend: no clear change in this variable here over 25 years.
  • Two places differ: the same variable is behaving differently in these two places.

"No significant trend" is a real finding, not a failure. The tool also shows where the answer is uncertain, because a 25-year record is short.

6. Who benefits

  • Residents: a plain answer about how rain, temperature, soil moisture and buildings are changing in their own town.
  • Students and teachers: a worked example of trend analysis on real NASA data in a place they know.
  • Councils and planners: climate variables next to building growth, to inform planning.
  • Researchers: a fast first look at which variables are changing where, before a deeper study.

7. Intended impact

  • Evidence instead of opinion. People can check a claim about local change against 25 years of data, and see whether it is statistically real.
  • Better understanding of "significant". Users learn that a line sloping upward is not always a real change, and that "no significant trend" is also an answer.
  • Informed local decisions. Councils, schools and researchers get the same open facts, with the uncertainty shown.
  • Reusable anywhere. Because the scripts and dataset versions are public, another team can rebuild EarthWatch for their own region.

8. What makes it creative and a strong use of data

Most trend tools make the user choose a variable first and then read a chart. EarthWatch turns that around: it tells the user which variables are changing in their place, shows where the same variable goes opposite ways, and puts every result into one plain sentence.

  1. Mission and model data together. Satellite rain, modelled land variables and building maps sit side by side, and the user decides what to compare.
  2. It helps with selection. The "what is changing here?" list points users to the variables that show change.
  3. It shows regional contrast. Two-colour trend maps make opposite trends in different places visible.
  4. Accessible. A link, a click, a sentence. No files, no code.
  5. Honest statistics. Significance, uncertainty, and the tool's limits are visible on the page.
  6. Reproducible. Scripts, exact dataset versions and dates are public, and every number can be regenerated.
